items.title: Postoperative changes in cardiovascular metrics and adverse clinical outcomes after major noncardiac surgery: a scoping review
items.summary: Cardiovascular metrics such as HR and BP reflect autonomic and haemodynamic regulation and are associated with perioperative risk. In noncardiac surgery, most work focuses on the intraoperative period or broad perioperative BP management, rather than the immediate postoperative period as a distinct window of vulnerability. The early postoperative period is characterised by residual anaesthetic effects, pain, fluid shifts, bleeding risk, inflammatory stress, mobilisation, and changing monitoring intensity.

items.title: Bleeding management in cardiac surgery: a simplified, goal-directed algorithm using conventional coagulation assays
items.summary: Excessive bleeding remains a major challenge in cardiac surgery despite advances in perioperative bleeding management, including the adoption of viscoelastic haemostatic assay (VHA)-guided algorithms. We propose an alternative, streamlined approach that primarily uses familiar, low-cost coagulation assays to rapidly identify and treat the principal post-cardiopulmonary bypass coagulation defects, reserving VHA for refractory bleeding, and prioritises factor concentrates as first-line therapy instead of allogeneic blood products.

items.title: Survival is not enough: from perioperative indicators to meaningful recovery
items.summary: Wanyonyi-Kay and colleagues developed a perioperative indicator framework (Perioperative Framework) using a systematic review, Delphi approach, and multidisciplinary consensus. They reduced 615 candidate measures to 28 core and 28 desirable structure and process indicators. The framework prioritises feasibility and patient-centred care while limiting measurement burden. We argue that these indicators should be linked to patient-important outcomes, such as neurocognitive and functional recovery. items.title: The path to propofol unresponsiveness has a starting point: paradoxical excitation might be the complex walk to get there
items.summary: Whether patients will experience paradoxical excitation at low doses of propofol can be predicted by the baseline type II complexity of the EEG. Paradoxical excitation appears to emerge when patients with a higher baseline type II complexity initially move towards lower levels.

items.title: Hypothalamic orexin input to the medial amygdala promotes arousal from anaesthesia and modulates exploratory behaviour
items.summary: Emergence from general anaesthesia is often accompanied by agitation, suggesting that recovery of consciousness can engage neural circuits that regulate arousal and behavioural responsiveness. The amygdala influences social, defensive, and exploratory behaviours, but whether orexinergic input to the amygdala regulates anaesthetic state transitions together with behavioural responses remains unclear.
